title: NASA Announces the X-70, a New Experimental Aircraft
paragraphs: With little fanfare beyond a stage at the Kennedy Space Center, NASA on 4 November introduced the X-70 Fractal, the newest heir to a lineage that runs from the Bell X-1 through the X-15 to the X-59. The crewed aircraft is pitched as a nimble research platform whose chief virtue is adaptability: a means of hurrying promising aviation technologies out of the laboratory and into the unforgiving test of real flight.

The numbers are unglamorous but telling. It can carry up to 2,000 pounds of experimental payloads, inside or out, swapped at short notice; it weighs 10,000 pounds at takeoff, cruises at Mach 0.75, climbs to 45,000 feet and flies about 1,500 nautical miles. NASA says its flight-control and manoeuvrability experiments will go beyond anything shown in crewed flight, and Laurie Grindle, who leads the agency's aeronautics division, said it was "exciting to bring on another X-plane".

For all that, the X-70 remains a paper aeroplane in everything but name. It has not flown, and Administrator Jared Isaacman would say only that a first flight under NASA's banner is expected within two years, an estimate rather than a commitment. The release names neither a builder nor a price tag, and the accompanying images are computer-generated, which leaves observers weighing ambition against evidence.

questions.q: What is the central appeal of the X-70?
questions.a: Its adaptability for rapidly testing new aviation technologies.

questions.q: How firm is the first-flight date?
questions.a: Not firm; it is an expectation of within two years.

questions.q: What does 'a paper aeroplane in everything but name' suggest?
questions.a: That the plane exists mostly as a plan and has not yet flown.
